analysis.one_liner: Strips health and dental insurers of their exemption from federal antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 416-7 in March 2017, but the Senate Judiciary Committee never acted on it, so the health insurance antitrust exemption remained in place.
analysis.plain_summary: Health insurers have long been exempt from federal antitrust laws under a 1945 law called the McCarran-Ferguson Act. This bill would remove that exemption for health and dental insurance, so that insurers could be sued for practices like colluding with providers on network pay rates. The House passed it overwhelmingly, but the Senate took no action, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy health or dental insurance would gain if the bill passed, because insurers could no longer rely on the McCarran-Ferguson Act to escape antitrust scrutiny for conduct like agreeing with providers on reimbursement rates or coordinating on network design. Federal enforcers and private plaintiffs could challenge such practices under the same antitrust laws that apply to other industries.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with health and dental insurance

how_it_helps.text: Declares that the McCarran-Ferguson Act no longer shields the business of health insurance — including dental insurance — from federal antitrust laws.
Applies prohibitions on unfair methods of competition to health insurers whether or not they operate for profit, closing a loophole for nonprofit insurers.
Leaves intact only narrow collaborative activities: sharing historical claims data, computing loss development factors, actuarial services not restraining trade, and voluntary standard policy forms.

analysis.who_pays: Health and dental insurers would bear the cost of antitrust exposure and potential litigation and damages. Any resulting pressure on insurer-provider negotiations could raise or lower premiums depending on market; supporters argued consumers would ultimately pay less through more competition.

drawbacks.text: The bill as amended carves out insurers' collaborative activities — sharing historical claims data, computing loss development factors, performing actuarial services, and developing standard policy forms — so the antitrust shield is stripped only partially, not fully.
It covers only health and dental insurance; life insurance and property/casualty lines keep their McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption, so the fix is narrower than a full repeal.

Opponents argued (via the failed motion to recommit on protecting affordable coverage for older Americans) that increasing competitive pressure on insurers could destabilize markets for older, sicker consumers, an objection the House majority rejected 233-189.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: repealing the antitrust exemption for health insurance could allow challenge to provider-network collusion and other anticompetitive conduct, potentially lowering premiums. The carve-outs preserve the industry's ability to share claims data and standardize policy forms, which insurers argue keeps the market efficient; that concession blunts much of the bill's force. The main cost is a modest loss of the safe harbor insurers have used for joint activities, which supporters of the exemption contend could raise costs. On balance the bill leaned toward consumers, but the Senate never gave it the vote that would have settled the question.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it overwhelmingly in March 2017, but the Senate referred it to its Judiciary Committee, which never acted, so it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill in March 2017 after a hearing and markup, and the Rules Committee gave it a closed rule blocking floor amendments.
The House passed it 416-7 on March 22, 2017, with 235 of 236 Republicans and 181 of 193 Democrats in favor.
A Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions to add protections for older Americans' health coverage failed 189-233, with only 2 Republicans crossing over.
The Senate received the bill on March 23, 2017 and referred it to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where no further action is recorded.
The bill never became law; the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 without Senate action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, who kept their special exemption from federal antitrust laws because the Senate never took up the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, who kept their antitrust exemption

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through House Judiciary.

House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a subcommittee hearing, discharged the subcommittee, marked up the bill, and reported it by voice vote.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (115th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill and never took it up, leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

against.name: Health insurance industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the original bill and pressed for the carve-outs that were added before House passage.

against.what_they_did: Rejected the Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions to add protections for older Americans' health coverage.

sides.party_line_note: Passage was near-unanimous (235 of 236 Republicans and 181 of 193 Democrats in favor), while the failed motion to recommit split sharply by party: 187 of 193 Democrats for it, 233 of 236 Republicans against.

industries.note: The bill would strip their special exemption from federal antitrust law, exposing mergers and conduct like provider-network collusion to Sherman Act and FTC challenges. Their carve-outs for data sharing and standard forms keep much of their collaborative machinery intact.

industries.industry: Consumers of health and dental coverage
industries.note: Greater antitrust enforcement against insurer collusion and consolidation could lower premiums and expand choice. This is the public the bill's title names as its beneficiary.
